title: Sleep in peace (Psalm 4)
hookLine: a psalm for night prayer: in peace I will sleep and I will rest

cards: It's one in the morning. The house is quiet, and your brain isn't. You're replaying a conversation from this afternoon, the thing they said, the thing you should have said back.
You rehearse the perfect reply, then rehearse it again. You check the time. You turn the pillow over to the cool side.
Long ago, somebody lay awake in a bed like this one, and wrote a song about it. The Church has been singing that song at bedtime for centuries.

teach.h: A NIGHT PSALM, PRAYED AT COMPLINE.
teach.b: Psalm 4 is a night psalm. For centuries it was prayed at Compline, the Church's last prayer before sleep, and in today's Liturgy of the Hours it's still there on Saturday nights. It starts in trouble.
"When I called upon him, the God of my justice heard me: when I was in distress, thou hast enlarged me." Enlarged: in Hebrew, God made room for me.
Distress is a tight place, a narrow corner, and the prayer remembers a time God gave it space.
Then the line for everyone lying awake angry. In the Douay-Rheims: "Be angry, and sin not: the things you say in your hearts, be sorry for them upon your beds." It doesn't say don't be angry.
It says be angry, and don't let the anger turn into harm. And those speeches you make in your head at one in the morning?
The Douay says, be sorry for them upon your beds; the Hebrew says something closer to be still there.
Saint Paul quotes the first half of that line to the Ephesians, and adds his own: don't let the sun go down on your anger.

teach.h: SLEEP AS AN ACT OF TRUST.
teach.b: The psalm ends with the line the whole night is waiting for: "In peace in the selfsame I will sleep, and I will rest." In the selfsame is an old, hard phrase; it seems to mean at once, or together.
Not after everything is fixed. Not after you win the argument. The one praying has the same enemies and the same worries, and still decides to lie down and trust.
Sleep, in this psalm, is an act of faith.

how: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours pray Psalm 4 at Night Prayer (Compline) on Saturday nights; for centuries it was part of Compline every night, the Church's last prayer before sleep.

o: resting only once your troubles are solved
lying down trusting, before all is fixed
a gentle wish spoken over the dead

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: God made room in a tight place

s: it says be angry, and sin not, and let the heart's speeches go quiet on your bed.
Saint Paul quotes Psalm 4 in his letter to the Ephesians
he quotes be angry, and sin not, and adds: don't let the sun go down on your anger.
the psalm's author sleeps only after his troubles are solved
he lies down in peace with the same worries, trusting.

games.q: it's one in the morning and you're lying awake, rehearsing a furious reply to someone. what does Psalm 4 tell you to do?
o: get up and send the reply now.
be angry, but don't sin; say it in your heart and let it go quiet on your bed.
pretend you aren't angry at all.
games.why: be angry, and sin not: the things you say in your hearts, be sorry for them upon your beds. the psalm allows the anger and asks you to lay it down.

practice: Find tonight's unfinished conversation, the one most likely to keep you up, and don't solve it: say it in your heart, the way the psalm says, and let it be quiet.
Then try the line for when the light goes off: in peace I will sleep, and I will rest. If you pray, say it to God; if you don't, let it be a way of putting the day down.

wordCard.voice: Sleep in peace. The last line of Psalm 4, a night prayer that lies down before everything is fixed. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: in peace, the first word of the psalm's last verse.

carryVoice: Your line: in peace I will sleep. Tomorrow's arguments can wait for tomorrow. Sleep well.
